It represents a part-whole relationship with strong ownership. Differences:</strong></p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Aspect</th>\n<th>Composition</th>\n<th>Aggregation</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody><tr>\n<td><strong>Relationship Type</strong></td>\n<td>Strong Perspective:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Composition</strong>: Parent object contains child objects in memory</li>\n<li><strong>Aggregation</strong>: Parent object contains references to child objects</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>When to Use Which:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Use Composition</strong> when child cannot exist without parent (Car-Engine, House-Room)</li>\n<li><strong>Use Aggregation</strong> when child can exist independently (Team-Player, Library-Book)</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Real-world Analogies:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Composition</strong>: Human body and the structure that shows the relationships between parent classes (superclasses) and child classes (subclasses) in an object-oriented system. It represents how classes inherit properties and methods from their ancestors, forming a tree-like structure.</p>\n<p><strong>Key Concepts:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Base/Parent/Super Class</strong>: The class being inherited from</li>\n<li><strong>Derived/Child/Sub Class</strong>: The class that inherits</li>\n<li><strong>Root Class</strong>: The topmost class in hierarchy</li>\n<li><strong>Leaf Classes</strong>: Classes with no children</li>\n<li><strong>Depth</strong>: Number of levels in inheritance chain</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>JavaScript Implementation:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Abstract Class:</strong> Can contain both abstract and concrete methods with implementations</li>\n<li><strong>Interface:</strong> Contains only method signatures (declarations) without implementations</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>2. Inheritance:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Abstract Class:</strong> Supports single inheritance only</li>\n<li><strong>Interface:</strong> Supports multiple inheritance</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>3. Access Modifiers:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Abstract Class:</strong> Can have various access modifiers (public, private, protected)</li>\n<li><strong>Interface:</strong> All methods are implicitly public</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>4. Variables:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Abstract Class:</strong> Can have instance variables, static variables, and constants</li>\n<li><strong>Interface:</strong> Can only have public, static, final constants</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>5. Constructor:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Abstract Class:</strong> Can have constructors</li>\n<li><strong>Interface:</strong> Cannot have constructors</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>JavaScript Comparison This allows a derived class to combine functionality from multiple base classes.</p>\n<p><strong>Key Characteristics:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>One child class inherits from multiple parent determined at runtime based on the actual type of the object, rather than at compile time. This is the foundation of polymorphism in object-oriented programming.</p>\n<p><strong>Key Features:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Method resolution happens at runtime</li>\n<li>Enables polymorphism and virtual function calls</li>\n<li>The actual method called depends on the object&#39;s runtime type</li>\n<li>Opposite of static binding (early binding)</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>JavaScript table of method pointers</li>\n<li><strong>Runtime Lookup:</strong> When a method is called, the system looks up the actual implementation</li>\n<li><strong>Type Resolution:</strong> The method called depends on the object&#39;s actual type, not the reference type</li>\n</ol>\n<p><strong>Example of Method Resolution:</strong></p>\n<div class=\"code\"><div class=\"code-head\"><span>css</span><button class=\"copy\" type=\"button\">Copy</button></div><pre><code class=\"hljs\">Employee reference -&gt; Points <i class=e>to</i> Manager <i class=e>object</i>\n                   -&gt; Method call: <i class=b>calculateSalary</i>()\n                   -&gt; Runtime lookup: Manager.<i class=b>calculateSalary</i>()\n                   -&gt; Executes Manager<i class=s>&#x27;s implementation</i></code></pre></div>\n<p><strong>Benefits:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>True Polymorphism:</strong> Same interface, different behaviors</li>\n<li><strong>Extensibility:</strong> New types can be added without changing existing code</li>\n<li><strong>Flexibility:</strong> Behavior can be determined at runtime</li>\n<li><strong>Code Reusability:</strong> Write code once, works with multiple types</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Use Cases:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Plugin systems where behavior is loaded at runtime</li>\n<li>GUI frameworks with different widget implementations</li>\n<li>Game engines with various entity types</li>\n<li>Framework design where users provide implementations</li>\n</ul>"},{"q":"What is static binding?","g":[],"a":"<p><strong>Static Binding</strong> (also called Early Binding) is a mechanism where the method to be called is determined at compile time based on the reference type, not the actual object type. The compiler resolves method calls during compilation.</p>\n<p><strong>Key Features:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Method resolution happens at compile time</li>\n<li>Based on the reference/pointer type, not object type</li>\n<li>Faster execution as no runtime lookup is needed</li>\n<li>Default behavior for non-virtual methods</li>\n<li>Opposite of dynamic binding (late binding)</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>JavaScript Example:</strong></p>\n<div class=\"code\"><div class=\"code-head\"><span>javascript</span><button class=\"copy\" type=\"button\">Copy</button></div><pre><code class=\"hljs\"><i class=c>// Note: JavaScript is dynamically typed, so true static binding</i>\n<i class=c>// doesn&#x27;t exist like in C++. Characteristics:</strong></p>\n<p><strong>Advantages:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Performance:</strong> Faster execution (no runtime lookup)</li>\n<li><strong>Predictability:</strong> Method calls are resolved at compile time</li>\n<li><strong>Memory Efficiency:</strong> No need for virtual function tables</li>\n<li><strong>Compile-time Optimization:</strong> Compiler can inline methods</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Disadvantages:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Less Flexibility:</strong> Cannot achieve runtime polymorphism</li>\n<li><strong>Limited Extensibility:</strong> Behavior is fixed at compile time</li>\n<li><strong>No Dynamic Dispatch:</strong> Same method always called regardless of object type</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>When Static Binding Occurs:</strong></p>\n<ol>\n<li><strong>Non-virtual functions</strong> in C++ (default behavior)</li>\n<li><strong>Private methods</strong> (cannot be overridden)</li>\n<li><strong>Static methods</strong> (belong to class, not instance)</li>\n<li><strong>Constructor calls</strong> (resolved at compile time)</li>\n<li><strong>Direct method calls</strong> without inheritance involved</li>\n</ol>\n<p><strong>Comparison with Dynamic Binding:</strong></p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Aspect</th>\n<th>Static Binding</th>\n<th>Dynamic Binding</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody><tr>\n<td>Resolution Time</td>\n<td>Compile Time</td>\n<td>Runtime</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Performance</td>\n<td>Faster</td>\n<td>Slower (lookup overhead)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Flexibility</td>\n<td>Limited</td>\n<td>High</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Polymorphism</td>\n<td>No</td>\n<td>Yes</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Memory Usage</td>\n<td>Less</td>\n<td>More (v-table)</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Method Called</td>\n<td>Based on reference type</td>\n<td>Based on object type</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody></table>\n<p><strong>Real-world Example:</strong></p>\n<div class=\"code\"><div class=\"code-head\"><span>javascript</span><button class=\"copy\" type=\"button\">Copy</button></div><pre><code class=\"hljs\"><i class=c>// In C++ Vehicle::startEngine</i>\n\n<i class=c>// Dynamic binding (virtual function)</i>\nvehicle-&gt;<i class=f>performChecks</i>();   <i class=c>// Calls Car::performChecks</i></code></pre></div>\n<p>This Principles:</strong></p>\n<p><strong>1. Static Context Limitations:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>No <code>this</code>/<code>self</code> reference available</li>\n<li>Cannot directly access instance members</li>\n<li>Must work through object references</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>2. Same-Class Access Rights:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Static methods can access <strong>all private static members</strong></li>\n<li>Static methods can access <strong>private instance members through object references</strong></li>\n<li>Access is granted because they&#39;re in the <strong>same class</strong></li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>3. The scope is <strong>not limited to object instances</strong> but extends to <strong>all instances of the same class</strong>.</p>\n<p><strong>Key Scope Rules:</strong></p>\n<ol>\n<li><strong>Same Class</strong>: All methods can access private members</li>\n<li><strong>Same Class, Different Objects</strong>: Can access private members of other instances</li>\n<li><strong>Subclasses</strong>: Cannot access private members (inheritance doesn&#39;t grant access)</li>\n<li><strong>Different Classes</strong>: Cannot access private members</li>\n<li><strong>Same Package/Namespace</strong>: Still cannot access (private overrides package visibility)</li>\n</ol>\n<p><strong>Java Example - Comprehensive Scope Demo:</strong></p>\n<div class=\"code\"><div The compiler determines which function to call based on the arguments provided.</p>\n<p><strong>Key Rules:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Same function name, different parameters</li>\n<li>Parameters can Example:</strong></p>\n<div class=\"code\"><div class=\"code-head\"><span>cpp</span><button class=\"copy\" type=\"button\">Copy</button></div><pre><code class=\"hljs\"><i class=k>class</i> <i This enables objects to work with operators in a natural and intuitive way.</p>\n<p><strong>Key Concepts:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Provides custom behavior for operators with user-defined types</li>\n<li>Makes code more readable and intuitive</li>\n<li>Can be implemented as member functions or friend functions</li>\n<li>Some operators cannot be overloaded (::, ., .*, ?:, This is because virtual functions require an object to exist with a vtable (virtual function table), but during constructor execution, the object is still being created and the vtable is not yet fully established.</p>\n<p><strong>Why constructors cannot be virtual:</strong></p>\n<ol>\n<li><strong>Object doesn&#39;t exist yet</strong>: Virtual functions need an existing object with a Tight Coupling</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Child classes become dependent on parent implementation</li>\n<li>Changes to parent class can break child classes</li>\n<li>Difficult to modify base classes without affecting derived classes</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>2. Inflexibility</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Hard to change inheritance hierarchy later</li>\n<li>Cannot inherit from multiple classes in many languages</li>\n<li>May inherit unwanted methods and properties</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>3. Deep Inheritance Hierarchies</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Creates complex, hard-to-understand code</li>\n<li>Performance overhead from method lookups</li>\n<li>Difficult debugging and maintenance</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>4. Fragile Base Class Problem</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Minor changes in base class can have unexpected effects</li>\n<li>Hard to predict all consequences of base class modifications</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>JavaScript Example (Showing Problems):</strong></p>\n<div class=\"code\"><div class=\"code-head\"><span>javascript</span><button class=\"copy\" Barbara Liskov in 1987, is the third of the five SOLID principles. In plain language: “If a program is using a pointer or reference to a base class, it must remain completely unaware whether that object is an instance of the base class or any of its derived classes.”</p>\n<p>Formal statement<br>Let Φ(x) be a property provable about objects x of type T. Then Φ(y) should also be true for objects y of type S, where S is a subtype of T.</p>\n<p>Rules distilled</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Method signatures<br>• Parameter types: contravariant (same or broader).<br>• Return types: covariant (same or narrower). </li>\n<li>Preconditions cannot be strengthened in the subtype. </li>\n<li>Postconditions cannot be weakened in the subtype. </li>\n<li>Invariants of the base type must be preserved. </li>\n<li>History rule: the subtype must not allow states that the base type disallows (e.g., mutating read-only fields). </li>\n<li>Exceptions: only subtypes of declared exceptions (or none) may be raised.</li>\n</ol>\n<p>Common pitfalls<br>• Square/Rectangle problem: forcing width and height to stay equal in Square breaks Rectangle invariants.<br>• Mutable etc.). </li>\n<li>Instance data (all fields, including inherited ones). </li>\n<li>Possible padding for alignment.</li>\n</ol>\n<p>Inheritance simply concatenates the ancestor fields to the derived fields, so the object grows. Each additional parent level adds its own fields. In languages with virtual dispatch, there is also a hidden pointer to the virtual method table (v-ptr).</p>\n<p>Python deep dive<br>CPython objects consist of:<br>• PyObject_HEAD (refcnt + type pointer)<br>• Optional dict or slots for attributes<br>• Inherited attributes are stored in the exact same dict/slot structure, not duplicated per class.</p>\n<p>Example</p>\n<div class=\"code\"><div class=\"code-head\"><span>python</span><button class=\"copy\" type=\"button\">Copy</button></div><pre><code class=\"hljs\"><i class=k>import</i> sys, gc, ctypes\n\n<i class=k>class</i> <i class=f>Base</i>:\n    <i class=k>def</i> <i class=f>__init__</i>(<i class=p>self</i>):\n        <i class=v>self</i>.a = <i class=n>1</i>\n        <i class=v>self</i>.b = <i class=n>2</i>\n\n<i class=k>class</i> <i class=f>Derived</i>(<i class=f>Base</i>):\n    <i class=k>def</i> <i class=f>__init__</i>(<i class=p>self</i>):\n        <i class=b>super</i>().__init__()\n        <i class=v>self</i>.c = <i class=n>3</i>\n        <i class=v>self</i>.d = <i class=n>4</i>\n\nb = Base()\nd = Derived()\n<i class=b>print</i>(<i class=s>&#x27;Base  size:&#x27;</i>, sys.getsizeof(b))        <i class=c># object + dict + attrs</i>\n<i class=b>print</i>(<i class=s>&#x27;Derived size:&#x27;</i>, sys.getsizeof(d))\n<i class=b>print</i>(<i class=s>&#x27;Base  dict:&#x27;</i>, sys.getsizeof(b.__dict__))\n<i class=b>print</i>(<i class=s>&#x27;Derived dict:&#x27;</i>, sys.getsizeof(d.__dict__))</code></pre></div>\n<p>Typical output on 64-bit CPython 3.11:<br>Base size: 56<br>Derived size: 56 # same object header<br>Base dict: 104 # 4 key/value pairs (2 + overhead)<br>Derived dict: 136 # 6 key/value pairs (4 + overhead)</p>\n<p>The object header stays constant; the dict inside grows by the number of attributes. Multiple inheritance adds an extra pointer per base class to the MRO cache, but this is per-class, not per-instance.</p>\n<p>JavaScript deep dive (V8)<br>Objects start as “hidden classes” (maps). Each time you add a new property, a new map is created that transitions from the old map. Inherited properties live in the prototype chain, not in the instance itself, so they do not increase instance size.</p>\n<p>Example</p>\n<div class=\"code\"><div class=\"code-head\"><span>javascript</span><button class=\"copy\" type=\"button\">Copy</button></div><pre><code class=\"hljs\"><i class=k>class</i> <i class=f>Base</i> {\n  <i class=f>constructor</i>(<i class=p></i>) { <i class=v>this</i>.<i class=v>a</i> = <i class=n>1</i>; <i class=v>this</i>.<i class=v>b</i> = <i class=n>2</i>; }\n}\n<i class=k>class</i> <i class=f>Derived</i> <i class=k>extends</i> <i class=f>Base</i> {\n  <i class=f>constructor</i>(<i class=p></i>) { <i class=v>super</i>(); <i class=v>this</i>.<i class=v>c</i> = <i class=n>3</i>; <i class=v>this</i>.<i class=v>d</i> = <i class=n>4</i>; }\n}\n\n<i class=k>const</i> b = <i class=k>new</i> <i class=f>Base</i>();\n<i class=k>const</i> d = <i class=k>new</i> <i class=f>Derived</i>();\n\n<i class=v>console</i>.<i class=f>log</i>(%<i class=f>HaveSameMap</i>(b, d)); <i class=c>// false in d8</i>\n<i class=v>console</i>.<i class=f>log</i>(%<i class=f>DebugPrint</i>(b));      <i class=c>// see instance size</i>\n<i class=v>console</i>.<i class=f>log</i>(%<i class=f>DebugPrint</i>(d));      <i class=c>// see instance size</i></code></pre></div>\n<p>In V8’s heap snapshot you will see:<br>• Base object: 4 properties → 32 bytes (on 64-bit)<br>• Derived object: 6 properties → 48 bytes (header + inline properties)</p>\n<p>Prototype properties such as methods are not duplicated per instance; they sit in the prototype object that is shared.</p>\n<p>Memory layout sketch (64-bit)<br>Base instance:<br>[ hidden-class ptr ][ properties array ptr ][ in-object a ][ in-object b ]<br>Derived instance:<br>[ hidden-class ptr ][ properties array ptr ][ a ][ b ][ c ][ d ]</p>\n<p>Impact of depth<br>Every level of inheritance adds its own fields to the object. Shallow inheritance keeps objects smaller. Deep hierarchies can also slow down property access because of longer prototype chains or MRO lookups.</p>\n<p>Garbage collection<br>Both Python and JavaScript use tracing GC. Larger objects mean more bytes walked by the GC, but the per-instance overhead is dominated by the attribute store, not inheritance metadata.</p>\n<p>Best practices<br>• Prefer composition over deep inheritance to keep object size minimal.<br>• Use <strong>slots</strong> in Python when the set of attributes is fixed to avoid per-instance dicts.<br>• In JavaScript, place shared data on the prototype to avoid duplication.</p>\n<p>Take-away<br>Inheritance increases the size of each instance by the sum of all ancestor fields. Language runtimes optimize method storage, but not data storage, so every additional field in the hierarchy is paid for by every object.</p>"},{"q":"What is the base class constructor call in derived class?","g":[],"a":"<p>Why it exists<br>A derived object is a single contiguous block of memory that embeds both the base part and the derived part. is the mechanism by which a programming language determines which specific method implementation to execute when a method is called. It&#39;s the process of selecting the appropriate method based on the runtime type of the object (dynamic dispatch) or compile-time information (static dispatch).</p>\n<p><strong>Types of Method Dispatch:</strong></p>\n<ol>\n<li><strong>Static Dispatch (Early Binding)</strong> - Resolved at compile time</li>\n<li><strong>Dynamic Dispatch (Late Binding)</strong> - Resolved at runtime</li>\n<li><strong>Single Dispatch</strong> - Based on one object&#39;s type</li>\n<li><strong>Multiple Dispatch</strong> - Based on multiple objects&#39; types</li>\n</ol>\n<p><strong>Python inheritance hierarchies.</p>\n<p><strong>Upcasting (Implicit Casting):</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Converting from a subclass to a superclass</li>\n<li>Always safe and automatic</li>\n<li>Loses access to is the difference between abstract class and concrete class?","g":[],"a":"<p>Abstract classes and concrete classes serve different purposes in object-oriented programming. An abstract class cannot be instantiated and may contain abstract methods, while a concrete class can be instantiated and must provide implementations for all its methods.</p>\n<p><strong>Key Differences:</strong></p>\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>\n<th>Aspect</th>\n<th>Abstract Class</th>\n<th>Concrete Class</th>\n</tr>\n</thead>\n<tbody><tr>\n<td>Instantiation</td>\n<td>Cannot be instantiated directly</td>\n<td>Can be instantiated</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Abstract Methods</td>\n<td>Can have abstract methods</td>\n<td>Cannot have abstract methods</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Implementation</td>\n<td>May have partial implementation</td>\n<td>Must have complete implementation</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Purpose</td>\n<td>Template/base for other classes</td>\n<td>Fully functional class</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td>Inheritance</td>\n<td>Must be extended to be used</td>\n<td>Can be used directly or extended</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody></table>\n<p><strong>Java Example:</strong></p>\n<div class=\"code\"><div class=\"code-head\"><span>java</span><button class=\"copy\" type=\"button\">Copy</button></div><pre><code class=\"hljs\"><i class=c>// Abstract Class</i>\n<i class=k>abstract</i> <i class=k>class</i> <i class=f>Animal</i> {\n    <i class=k>protected</i> String name;\n    <i class=k>protected</i> <i class=t>int</i> age;\n    \n    <i class=c>// Constructor in abstract class</i>\n    <i class=t>public</i> <i class=f>Animal</i><i class=p>(String name, <i class=t>int</i> age)</i> {\n        <i class=b>this</i>.name = name;\n        <i class=b>this</i>.age = age;\n    }\n    \n    <i class=c>// Concrete method (has implementation)</i>\n    <i class=k>public</i> <i class=t>void</i> <i class=f>sleep</i><i class=p>()</i> {\n        System.out.println(name + <i class=s>&quot; to/from byte streams</li>\n<li><strong>Cloneable</strong> - Objects that support cloning/copying </li>\n<li><strong>Remote</strong> - Objects that can be used in remote method invocation</li>\n<li><strong>EventListener</strong> - Objects that can handle events</li>\n<li><strong>Cacheable</strong> - Objects suitable for caching</li>\n<li><strong>Immutable</strong> - Objects whose state cannot be modified</li>\n</ol>\n<p><strong>Key Benefits:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Type Safety</strong>: Compile/runtime checks for specific capabilities</li>\n<li><strong>Framework Integration</strong>: Frameworks can treat objects differently based on markers</li>\n<li><strong>Documentation</strong>: Self-documenting code about object capabilities </li>\n<li><strong>Flexibility</strong>: Easy to add/remove capabilities without changing method signatures</li>\n<li><strong>Polymorphism</strong>: Different behavior based on interface implementation</li>\n</ul>\n<p><strong>Key Points:</strong></p>\n<ul>\n<li>Marker interfaces contain no methods or fields</li>\n<li>They serve as metadata/tags for classes</li>\n<li>Used extensively in frameworks for capability detection</li>\n<li>Enable polymorphic behavior based on type checking</li>\n<li>Common in serialization, caching, and event handling systems</li>\n</ul>"}]
